info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 7.2: Rendering by Rule: XSLT, CETEIcean, and Print Stylesheets.

questiontext.text: Why is Tuesday's hand-made page not enough to publish your whole edition?

generalfeedback.text: A hand-made page shows what each element should become; today you turn each of those decisions into a rule that renders the whole file automatically.

answer.text: It covers only a sample of lines and falls out of date every time the TEI file changes; rules can render the whole file again in seconds.

feedback.text: Correct. The hand-made page shows what each element should become; rules apply those decisions everywhere, every time.

answer.text: Hand-written HTML is not valid in modern browsers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tuesday's page is ordinary, valid HTML. The problem is scale and upkeep, not validity.

answer.text: Hand-made pages cannot include CSS.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tuesday's page used two stylesheets.

answer.text: The TEI Consortium forbids publishing hand-written HTML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such rule. Hand-written pages simply do not scale.

questiontext.text: Your stylesheet drops every <gap/> from the reading view. What does determinism tell you about this error?

generalfeedback.text: A deterministic stylesheet gives identical output every run, so every error can be traced to one rule or one line of TEI, but it will repeat a wrong rule just as faithfully as a right one.

answer.text: It will happen the same way on every run, and it can be traced to one rule, so fixing that rule fixes it everywhere.

feedback.text: Correct. Determinism makes errors traceable and repeatable; it does not make the rules correct.

answer.text: It cannot be an error, because deterministic programs are always correct.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A deterministic rule repeats a wrong decision just as faithfully as a right one.

answer.text: It will probably disappear if you run the stylesheet again.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The same input always gives the same output, so the gaps will be dropped again.

answer.text: It was caused by randomness in the browser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no randomness to blame; the cause is in the file or the rule.

questiontext.text: Besides publishing, what use of rendering did the cataloguing team described in the lesson find very helpful?

generalfeedback.text: Working projects render TEI with stylesheets both to publish their editions and to proofread their own encoding, and you can do both with today's tools.

answer.text: An HTML preview of each TEI record, which made proofreading easy on the spot.

feedback.text: Correct. Errors that hide among tags stand out in running text, so rendering is also an editor's checking tool.

answer.text: Automatic translation of each record into several languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The template produced an HTML preview, not translations.

answer.text: Replacing the TEI records with HTML so the XML could be deleted.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The TEI stayed the source; the HTML was a preview of it.

answer.text: Generating the TEI header automatically from images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The template transformed existing TEI into a preview page.

name.text: 04 Question: Two Routes from TEI to a Web Page

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly contrasts the two routes?

generalfeedback.text: XSLT turns TEI into HTML before you publish; CETEIcean turns it into HTML in the reader's browser; both apply your decisions, but they store them in different places.

answer.text: XSLT writes HTML files before publication; CETEIcean turns the TEI into HTML elements in the reader's browser each time the page opens.

feedback.text: Correct. Both apply your decisions, but at different times and from different places.

answer.text: XSLT works only in the browser; CETEIcean works only on your computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is the other way round: XSLT runs beforehand, CETEIcean runs in the browser.

answer.text: CETEIcean requires you to delete your TEI file after rendering.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CETEIcean needs your TEI file; it builds the page from it.

answer.text: The two routes produce identical files, so the choice makes no difference.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They store your decisions in different places, which shapes what can go wrong.

questiontext.text: What does <xsl:apply-templates/> do inside a template?

generalfeedback.text: An XSLT stylesheet is a list of templates; each matches one kind of TEI element and writes HTML in its place, then hands the element's contents on to other templates.

answer.text: It processes the current element's contents, handing each child to whatever template matches it.

feedback.text: Correct. That is how the processor moves inward through your file, template by template.

answer.text: It copies the whole TEI file unchanged into the output.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It processes contents with templates; it does not copy the file wholesale.

answer.text: It stops processing, so the element's contents are ignored.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It does the opposite: it continues processing inside the element.

answer.text: It applies Tuesday's CSS to the element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CSS is applied later by the browser; XSLT only writes the HTML.

name.text: 06 Question: Setting Up: Python, lxml, and a Small Script

questiontext.text: Why should the generated page be written into the rendering/ folder under a new name such as reading-auto.html?

generalfeedback.text: Install lxml, save the short render.py, and run it with your TEI file, a stylesheet and an output name; write the output beside Tuesday's CSS under a new name.

answer.text: So it can find Tuesday's CSS files beside it, and so it never overwrites the hand-made edition.html you need for comparison.

feedback.text: Correct. Location lets the stylesheet link work; a new name protects Tuesday's ground truth.

answer.text: Because lxml can only write files whose names end in -auto.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The name is your choice; the point is not to overwrite Tuesday's page.

answer.text: Because Python cannot write files at the top of a repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It can; the folder matters because the page links to CSS files there.

answer.text: Because Git ignores files in other folders.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tracks files in any folder of the repository.

name.text: 07 Question: The Built-in Rules: What Happens to Elements You Forget

questiontext.text: Your stylesheet has no template for <gap/>. What appears in the output where each gap was?

generalfeedback.text: An element with no template disappears and its text falls through as plain words; this glues both layers of a <choice> together and silently deletes empty elements such as <gap/>.

answer.text: Nothing at all; an empty element with no template vanishes without any warning.

feedback.text: Correct. The built-in rule processes the element's contents, and an empty element has none.

answer.text: The word gap in plain text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Element names are never written by the built-in rules; only text content falls through.

answer.text: An error message that stops the transformation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XSLT gives no error; that is what makes the loss dangerous.

answer.text: Brackets with the reason taken from the attributes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Only a template you write can produce that.

questiontext.text: You wrote match="choice", but your output shows both layers glued together. What is the most likely cause?

generalfeedback.text: Declare the TEI namespace with a tei: prefix and use it in every match; a template without the prefix never fires, and the built-in rules quietly take over.

answer.text: The template lacks the tei: prefix, so it never matches your TEI elements and the built-in rules take over.

feedback.text: Correct. A TEI <choice> and a <choice> in no namespace are different elements to the processor.

answer.text: Your TEI file is not well-formed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A badly formed file would fail to load at all, not render both layers.

answer.text: Tuesday's CSS is overriding the stylesheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CSS cannot add text; the glued words are in the generated HTML itself.

answer.text: XSLT always shows both layers of a <choice>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A correctly prefixed template can select just one layer.

questiontext.text: Why does the root template use <xsl:apply-templates select="//tei:body"/> rather than a bare <xsl:apply-templates/>?

generalfeedback.text: The root template writes the HTML shell, copies your title from the header, keeps charset and lang, and processes only the <body> so the header does not spill onto the page.

answer.text: So that only the body is processed; otherwise the text of the <teiHeader> would fall through onto the top of the page.

feedback.text: Correct. Selecting the body keeps catalogue information out of the reader's view.

answer.text: Because the body is the only part of a TEI file that contains text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The header contains plenty of text, which is exactly why it must be excluded.

answer.text: To make the page load faster in the browser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The point is what appears on the page, not speed.

answer.text: Because XSLT cannot read the header at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The same template reads the title from the header with xsl:value-of.

name.text: 10 Question: Structure: Divisions, Headings, and Paragraphs

questiontext.text: With the template <section class="{@type}">, what does <div type="clause"> become?

generalfeedback.text: Map divisions, headings and paragraphs to HTML equivalents, use {@type} to carry attribute values into classes, and give every structural element in your file its own template.

answer.text: <section class="clause">

feedback.text: Correct. The curly braces insert the value of the type attribute.

answer.text: <section class="{@type}">, copied literally.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inside an output attribute, curly braces are evaluated, not copied.

answer.text: <section class="div">

feedback.text: Incorrect. @type means the attribute's value, not the element's name.

answer.text: Nothing, because <div> has no HTML equivalent.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The template maps it to <section>.

name.text: 11 Question: Choosing a Layer: The <choice> Template

questiontext.text: Your reading stylesheet's <choice> template selects only tei:reg|tei:expan|tei:corr. Where are the original spellings in the generated page?

generalfeedback.text: A <choice> template that selects only one child writes one layer into the page; giving the output Tuesday's class names lets Tuesday's CSS style it unchanged.

answer.text: Nowhere; they were never processed, so they are not in the HTML at all.

feedback.text: Correct. Unlike Tuesday's page, the XSLT page drops the other layer instead of hiding it.

answer.text: Hidden by CSS, as on Tuesday.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is nothing to hide; the stylesheet never wrote them.

answer.text: In a tooltip on each regularized word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Only a template you write could add a tooltip.

answer.text: At the end of the page, in a list.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unselected children produce no output anywhere.

questiontext.text: What does the predicate in match="tei:hi[@rend='sup']" do?

generalfeedback.text: The reading stylesheet chooses <expan> and marks <ex> for italics; the diplomatic one chooses <abbr> and needs a predicate template for raised letters and every other <hi> your file uses.

answer.text: It limits the template to <hi> elements whose rend attribute is sup.

feedback.text: Correct. Other <hi> values need their own templates, or their text falls through unmarked.

answer.text: It makes every <hi> in the file superscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The square brackets narrow the match to one value of rend.

answer.text: It deletes the rend attribute from the TEI file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Stylesheets never change the source file.

answer.text: It expands the abbreviation automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Expansions come from your <expan>, chosen by the <choice> template.

questiontext.text: Why does the reading stylesheet write a line break's space with <xsl:text> </xsl:text>?

generalfeedback.text: In the diplomatic view each <lb/> becomes Tuesday's numbered span; in the reading view it becomes a protected space, except a break="no" break, which becomes nothing.

answer.text: Because XSLT normally discards bare whitespace in a stylesheet, and xsl:text protects the space so words do not glue together.

feedback.text: Correct. Without it, the last word of one line could join the first word of the next.

answer.text: Because HTML forbids ordinary spaces between words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTML uses ordinary spaces; the issue is that the stylesheet would drop the space.

answer.text: To insert a visible line break in the reading view.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reading view deliberately lets lines flow; only a space is written.

answer.text: To keep the line number in the reading view.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Line numbers belong to the diplomatic view.

questiontext.text: Your reading view shows Pro- vince with a space inside the word. What causes it?

generalfeedback.text: Whitespace before a break="no" line break survives as a stray space; a text template removes it, while the hyphen stays because it belongs to your transcription.

answer.text: The new line and indentation before the break="no" <lb/> in your XML survive as whitespace, even though the <lb/> itself writes nothing.

feedback.text: Correct. A text template that trims that whitespace rejoins the word.

answer.text: The hyphen was added by the stylesheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The hyphen is in your transcription; the stray space is the problem.

answer.text: The browser always adds a space after a hyphen.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The space comes from whitespace in your source file.

answer.text: The <lb/> template writes a space for every break.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The break="no" template writes nothing; the space was already in the file.

questiontext.text: Why does the generated tooltip read damage, 2 word(s) rather than damage, 2 words?

generalfeedback.text: Give <gap/> a template or it vanishes; attribute value templates can copy its reason and extent into both a tooltip and real text, exactly as written in your TEI.

answer.text: Because the stylesheet copies the attribute values exactly as written and knows nothing about English plurals.

feedback.text: Correct. A rule is only as smart as you make it.

answer.text: Because the TEI file is invalid.

feedback.text: Incorrect. unit="word" is the normal TEI value; the stylesheet simply copies it.

answer.text: Because tooltips cannot display the letter s.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tooltips display any text the HTML gives them.

answer.text: Because CETEIcean rewrote the attribute.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is the XSLT route; CETEIcean is not involved.

questiontext.text: Which change is NOT part of turning reading.xsl into diplomatic.xsl?

generalfeedback.text: Save reading.xsl, copy it to diplomatic.xsl with four changes and one extra template, and run both to produce full-length versions of both views.

answer.text: Editing the TEI file to remove every <reg>.

feedback.text: Correct. The source never changes; only the stylesheet's choices do.

answer.text: Linking diplomatic.css instead of reading.css.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is one of the four changes.

answer.text: Making the <choice> template select orig|abbr|sic.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is one of the four changes.

answer.text: Making each <lb/> write Tuesday's numbered span.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is one of the four changes.

name.text: 17 Question: Comparing the Generated Pages with Tuesday's

questiontext.text: In the page source, how does today's generated reading page differ from Tuesday's hand-made page?

generalfeedback.text: Compare the generated pages with Tuesday's both on screen and in the page source; the XSLT pages drop one layer entirely, so each view must link to the other.

answer.text: Tuesday's page contains both layers with one hidden by CSS; today's contains only the reading layer.

feedback.text: Correct. That is why each view should link to the other.

answer.text: They are identical in the page source; only the CSS differs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The XSLT page never wrote the original layer.

answer.text: Today's page contains both layers and Tuesday's contains one.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is the other way round.

answer.text: Today's page contains the TEI markup itself.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The XSLT route publishes ordinary HTML; it is CETEIcean that keeps TEI structure.

name.text: 18 Question: Generic Stylesheets Make Generic Decisions

questiontext.text: What does using a ready-made TEI stylesheet require of you?

generalfeedback.text: Ready-made stylesheets make display decisions without knowing your document, so using one means checking and overriding its choices rather than skipping your own.

answer.text: Checking each of its display decisions against your own table and overriding those that disagree.

feedback.text: Correct. A generic stylesheet moves the work; it does not remove your decisions.

answer.text: Nothing; it already knows your document's needs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It was written for many projects at once and knows nothing of your policies.

answer.text: Deleting your RENDERING.md, since the stylesheet replaces it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Your table is what you check the stylesheet against.

answer.text: Rewriting your TEI to match the stylesheet's expectations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The evidence should not bend to a display tool.

questiontext.text: What does CETEIcean turn <lb n="12"/> into?

generalfeedback.text: CETEIcean renames every TEI element as a tei- custom element and keeps both layers of every <choice>, leaving every display decision to your CSS.

answer.text: A custom element <tei-lb n="12">, with its attribute kept.

feedback.text: Correct. Every TEI element becomes a tei- element of the same name, in lower case.

answer.text: An HTML <br>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CETEIcean keeps your structure and renames elements; it does not map lb to br.

answer.text: Nothing; CETEIcean removes empty elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The element is kept, though being empty it shows nothing by itself.

answer.text: A numbered paragraph.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Any numbering must come from your CSS.

questiontext.text: You double-click ceteicean.html and see a blank page. What is the fix?

generalfeedback.text: A CETEIcean page loads the library and fetches your TEI file; it must be opened through a local web server, such as Python's http.server, not by double-clicking.

answer.text: Serve the folder with a local web server, such as python3 -m http.server 8000, and open the page through localhost.

feedback.text: Correct. Browsers block a page opened from disk from fetching your TEI file.

answer.text: Convert the TEI file to HTML first with XSLT.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is the other route; CETEIcean needs the TEI file itself.

answer.text: Delete the <teiHeader> from your TEI file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The header is not the problem; the browser refused to fetch the file.

answer.text: Rename the page to index.xml.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The page must stay HTML; it needs to be served, not renamed.

name.text: 21 Question: Styling tei- Elements: The Reading View

questiontext.text: Your CETEIcean page shows all your paragraphs and headings run together in one stream. Why?

generalfeedback.text: Browsers display custom elements inline, so your CSS must make every structural tei- element a block, and the layer rules are Tuesday's rules with tei- names.

answer.text: Browsers display custom elements inline, so tei-p and tei-head need display: block in your CSS.

feedback.text: Correct. Nothing is automatic for tei- elements; every structural element needs a display rule.

answer.text: CETEIcean deletes paragraph breaks from the TEI.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The structure is kept; the browser just does not know how to display it.

answer.text: Your TEI file has no <p> elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The elements are there as tei-p; they lack a display rule.

answer.text: The local web server strips line breaks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The server delivers the file unchanged.

name.text: 22 Question: The Diplomatic View and the Empty Gap

questiontext.text: How do you make gaps visible in a CETEIcean page?

generalfeedback.text: The diplomatic CSS reuses Tuesday's rules with tei- names and the kept n attribute; an empty <gap/> shows nothing until a behavior puts real brackets inside it.

answer.text: Add a behavior, such as c.addBehaviors({ tei: { gap: ["[…]"] } }), which puts real brackets inside every tei-gap.

feedback.text: Correct. An empty element shows nothing until a behavior gives it content.

answer.text: Nothing is needed; CETEIcean shows gaps automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. An empty tei-gap displays nothing by default.

answer.text: Write the brackets into your TEI file in place of <gap/>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would damage the encoding to fix a display problem.

answer.text: Set tei-gap { display: block; }.

feedback.text: Incorrect. An empty block is still empty.

questiontext.text: A reader's browser has JavaScript turned off. Which route still shows your edition?

generalfeedback.text: XSLT gives plain HTML with one layer chosen in advance; CETEIcean keeps your TEI in the page with every decision in CSS; choose the one you can maintain and record why.

answer.text: XSLT, because its output is plain HTML that needs no script.

feedback.text: Correct. CETEIcean builds the page with JavaScript, so it shows nothing without it.

answer.text: CETEIcean, because it uses the TEI file directly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CETEIcean is itself JavaScript.

answer.text: Both, because neither uses JavaScript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CETEIcean depends on JavaScript.

answer.text: Neither, because all web pages need JavaScript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Plain HTML and CSS work without it.

questiontext.text: Why does the print rule show the hidden gap-info text instead of adding the gap details with CSS content?

generalfeedback.text: Put print-only rules inside @media print, reveal on paper the gap details that tooltips carry on screen, and check every editorial mark in the print preview.

answer.text: Because the details are real text already in the HTML; the print rule only shows them, so they can be copied and read aloud.

feedback.text: Correct. Editorial meaning belongs in the HTML; CSS only changes whether it is visible.

answer.text: Because CSS cannot be used when printing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. @media print rules are CSS.

answer.text: Because tooltips print automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tooltips never appear on paper, which is the problem being solved.

answer.text: Because gap-info is required by the TEI Guidelines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is a class name chosen in the stylesheet.

questiontext.text: According to the lesson, what is the PDF of your edition?

generalfeedback.text: The browser's Save as PDF with a good print stylesheet makes a sound PDF; it is one more view of the same source, and this week's work feeds directly into the Print-Ready Publication.

answer.text: One more view generated from the same TEI source and rules, alongside the reading and diplomatic views on screen.

feedback.text: Correct. None of the outputs is the edition; the edition is the encoded file and the decisions that render it.

answer.text: The authoritative edition, which replaces the TEI file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The TEI remains the source; the PDF is an output.

answer.text: Something that can only be made with XSL-FO software.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The browser's Save as PDF with a print stylesheet is a sound route.

answer.text: A file that must be edited by hand after export.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editing the PDF by hand would break the link to your rules.

name.text: 26 Question: Worked Example: The 1791 Decree by XSLT

questiontext.text: Accented letters in Ace's generated page appear as pairs of strange symbols. What should be checked first?

generalfeedback.text: For a French text, set lang="fr", keep UTF-8 in both the output setting and the page head, and check every accented letter and every <choice> in both views.

answer.text: That xsl:output has encoding="utf-8" and the page head has <meta charset="utf-8"/>.

feedback.text: Correct. A missing encoding setting is the usual cause of garbled accents.

answer.text: That the page says lang="en".

feedback.text: Incorrect. The page should say lang="fr", but the language setting does not cause garbled letters.

answer.text: That every <choice> selects <orig>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Layer choice does not affect how letters are encoded.

answer.text: That the decree has no <div> elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Structure has nothing to do with character encoding.

name.text: 27 Question: Worked Example: The 1752 Treaty in CETEIcean

questiontext.text: Which difference from the decision table does the CETEIcean treaty example reveal?

generalfeedback.text: CETEIcean renders the treaty lines in both views with Tuesday's rules, but gap details stay hidden in attributes and split-word whitespace survives; record both against your table.

answer.text: Gap reasons and extents stay hidden in attributes, and split-word whitespace can survive as a stray space.

feedback.text: Correct. Both are fidelity gaps to record in RENDERING.md.

answer.text: The regularized spellings are lost entirely.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both layers are in the page; CSS chooses which to show.

answer.text: Line numbers cannot be shown at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The diplomatic CSS shows them from the kept n attribute.

answer.text: Unclear readings are deleted.

feedback.text: Incorrect. tei-unclear is styled with a dotted underline.

name.text: 28 Question: The Fidelity Audit: Tool Error or Undecided Decision?

questiontext.text: The generated page shows the text of a <note> on line 30 as plain words, and your RENDERING.md never mentions <note>. What kind of problem is this, and where is it fixed first?

generalfeedback.text: Sort every difference into a tool error, fixed in the rule, or an undecided decision, fixed first in RENDERING.md; a tool's default is never an editorial decision.

answer.text: An undecided decision; decide in RENDERING.md how notes should appear, then write the rule.

feedback.text: Correct. The tool's default chose for you; a default is never an editorial decision.

answer.text: A tool error; fix the stylesheet and leave RENDERING.md alone.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The rule could not carry out a decision that was never made.

answer.text: No problem; the tool's output is acceptable as it stands.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Whatever the tool did was not your choice.

answer.text: A transcription error; delete the <note> from the TEI.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The encoding is fine; the rendering decision is missing.

name.text: 29 Question: Hypothetical Scenario: The Vanishing Gap

questiontext.text: Which quick check would have caught the vanishing gap in the scenario?

generalfeedback.text: An empty element with no rule disappears without warning; counting each element in the TEI against its marks on the page catches the loss.

answer.text: Counting the <gap/> elements in the TEI against the brackets on the rendered page.

feedback.text: Correct. A count check takes a minute and catches silent losses.

answer.text: Validating the TEI file against the schema.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The TEI was valid; the loss happened in the rendering.

answer.text: Checking that the page looked clean.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A clean look was exactly what hid the problem.

answer.text: Running the stylesheet a second time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A deterministic stylesheet would drop the gap again.

questiontext.text: What does completing Step 2 give you for Friday?

generalfeedback.text: Completing Step 2 gives you runnable rules that render your whole document in both views, and an audit that separates tool errors from decisions you had not yet made.

answer.text: Runnable rules that render the whole document in both views, and an audit separating tool errors from decisions not yet made.

feedback.text: Correct. On Friday an AI-written stylesheet will be audited against Tuesday's page and today's rules.

answer.text: A finished, final edition that needs no further changes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The rendering will keep changing as your TEI and decisions develop.

answer.text: A replacement for Tuesday's decision table.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The rules carry out the table; they do not replace it.

answer.text: A PDF ready for submission.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Print-Ready Publication is due in December; today only starts it.
